newsitem.title: FRANCE: French stocks plunge on unexpected poll result.
newsitem.headline: French stocks plunge on unexpected poll result.

text.p: French shares plunged on Monday morning after a strong lead by the opposition left-wing parties in the first round of a parliamentary election on Sunday against expectations the governing centre-right coalition would win.
The blue-chip CAC-40 index opened down 106.03 points or 3.84 percent at 2,656.87 while the CAC-40 May futures contract was down at 2,670 from 2,761 at Friday's close.
The CAC-40 index was down 4.13 percent after five minutes of trading.

With most votes counted in metropolitan France, the Interior Ministry said the combined left had polled 40.1 percent, the RPR-UDF coalition and other right-wing candidates 36.5 percent and the National Front 15 percent. Ecologists scored 6.8 percent.
Most of the 577 National Assembly seats are set to go to a run-off on June 1, where the behaviour of Front supporters and of the 31.6 percent of voters who abstained will be crucial.
Financial markets had been expecting the centre-right to hold on to a reduced majority. "The market is going to be volatile all week," said a trader.

"The stock market, putting its trust in opinion polls showing the right would win, had treated the election as a non-event. We are going to pay for it because the market had not taken the political risk fully into account," a dealer said.

"We are faced with the worst possible scenario. Is the right going to return the votes in their favour in the second round? If the left wins, what is going to happen to the Maastricht Treaty? And what about issues such as Thomson ?," another dealer said. They added it was now necessary to protect one's money and sell even if the election result does not impact the fundamentals such as corporate results.
Eric Chaney, an economist at Morgan Stanley, told RFTV that he saw a two-stage fall in stockmarket, today and tomorrow when non-residents will sell what they bought before the first round.
U.S. and U.K. markets are closed today for public holidays.

"If there's a Socialist victory, the stockmarket will have to price in the fact that there will probably be new elections in France at the end of 1998," he said, noting President Jacques Chirac was likely to call another early election in 1998 to try and get rid of a left-wing government. "The markets would be more sceptical about economic growth and corporate investments...so we could have a very subdued stockmarket."

Christopher Potts, an analyst at brokerage Cheuvreux de Virieu, said that the stockmarket was the most sensitive to a change in government and he expected a "big fall as the risk of a change in government is priced in."
The SBF said that there were no limits on the blue-chip index.

On the MATIF futures and options market, however, there is the possibility to suspend trading when two contracts if two consecutive months are down by more than 120 points compared to the previous settlement. For the May contract this is 2,762 and for June it is 2,737.50.

Fantozzi stressed that the French election, which has a second round on June 1, was not yet decided.

But he said his sense of the results so far was that "it puts attention on the internal opinion of the French (electorate) being sceptical on EMU, and this will create attention to the national opinions of all countries involved".
